question.problem: Estimate $(1.06)^{4.1}$ using a differential $\text{d}f$ of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{y}$ at the point $(1,4).$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =y{x}^{y-1}\,\text{d}x+{x}^{y}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(1,4),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =4\cdot {1}^{3}\,\text{d}x+{1}^{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =4\,\text{d}x+0\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(1+Δx,4+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈4\,Δx+0\,Δy.
$$

Note that 

$$
(1.06)^{4.1}=f(1.06,4.1),
$$

so we want to move to the point $(1.06,4.1).$

Moving from $(1,4)$ to $(1.06,4.1),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =1.06-1=0.06, \\ Δy & =4.1-4=0.1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈4\cdot (0.06)+0\cdot (0.1) \\  & ≈0.24+0 \\  & ≈0.24\,.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that the value of $f$ increases by about $0.24.$ Consequently, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1.06,4.1) & ≈f(1,4)+0.24 \\ (1.06)^{4.1} & ≈{1}^{4}+0.24 \\  & ≈1+0.24 \\  & ≈1.24\,.\end{aligned}
$$
